_comment: Cambridge 0097's Thinking and Working Scientifically and Science in Context objectives for Stage 4 that no Grade 4 unit reached, authored as reasoning prompts. Added 2026-09-17 with the Stages 1-4 re-point. Stage 4 publishes 63 objectives against the 2018 framework's 34, and twenty-six of the 63 are TWS or SIC - Science in Context alone grows to five, all of them about the learner's OWN area and the people in it, which is why these prompts name charcoal, solar panels, the rift valley and a game warden rather than staying general. Three were claimed rather than authored, on content already in the units: 4TWSc.08 in Unit 3, whose worked example reads a thermometer every two minutes into a table; 4TWSp.04 in the same unit, whose waterproof method says 'to keep the test fair, drip the same number of water drops onto each material from the same height'; and 4TWSm.03 in Unit 6, which teaches circuit symbols as 'the secret code of scientists' and has the learner draw a circuit diagram. 4TWSp.04 gets a prompt as well as a claim, because the method identifies the variables FOR the learner and the objective asks the learner to identify them.
_vehicle: reasoningPrompts. See cambridge-stage1-enquiry.json for the full note on the deck-only section at Stages 1-4 and why appending is safe.
source: Authored 2026-09-17 against Cambridge 0097 Stage 4, anchored to the investigations in Grade 4 units 1-6.
_minimumCovered: One prompt per Stage 4 TWS/SIC objective that no unit's own content already delivers, plus one that reinforces a marginal claim. Coverage is a number that only goes up.

prompts.prompt: There are five kinds of scientific enquiry: research, fair testing, observing over time, identifying and classifying, and pattern seeking. Using the classification key was one of them. Which one, and which kind would you need to find out whether birds visit your yard more in the morning or the evening?
keyIdeas: A classification key is identifying and classifying
Counting birds morning and evening is pattern seeking
Nothing is changed by the investigator in either one
prompts.modelAnswer: The key is identifying and classifying: I answer yes-or-no questions to put an animal into a group, and I change nothing. The bird question is pattern seeking - I count at two times of day over several days and look for a pattern in the numbers, still changing nothing myself. Neither is a fair test, because in a fair test I change one thing on purpose.

prompts.prompt: You classified animals and described habitats. Name two people who work near you who use that same science, and say exactly what they use it for.
keyIdeas: A game warden or ranger identifies species and counts them
A vet identifies what kind of animal and what it needs
A fisherman classifies the catch and knows which is too young to take
prompts.modelAnswer: A game warden identifies species and counts them year by year, because a falling count is the first sign that a habitat is in trouble. A fisherman classifies the catch and puts back the fish that are too young, which keeps there being fish next year. Both of them are doing exactly what a classification key does, on work that other people depend on.

prompts.prompt: Turn this into a question you could actually investigate: 'solar energy is good'. Then say what you would measure.
keyIdeas: 'Good' cannot be measured; pick something that can
For example: does a solar lamp charge faster in direct sun than in shade?
Measure the time to charge, or how long it then lights
prompts.modelAnswer: 'Solar energy is good' is an opinion, so nothing could settle it. A question I could investigate is: does a solar lamp charge faster in direct sunlight than in the shade? I would measure the time each one takes to charge fully, or how many hours it lights afterwards. A scientific question names something you can measure and says what would count as an answer.

prompts.prompt: You surveyed your home and found 6 devices using electrical energy, 3 using light, 2 using heat and 1 using movement. Say how you would show this as a table, as a bar chart and as a dot plot, and which one you would choose to convince your family to save energy.
keyIdeas: Table: one row per form, one column for the count
Bar chart: one bar per form, height is the count
Dot plot: one dot per device above its form
The bar chart makes the biggest group obvious
prompts.modelAnswer: The table has a row for each form of energy and a column for how many devices. The bar chart has one bar per form with its height as the count. The dot plot puts one dot for each device above its form, so twelve dots in four stacks. I would use the bar chart to convince my family, because the electrical bar is twice the next one and that is visible in a second - and I would say that is where saving would matter most.

prompts.prompt: Charcoal and solar panels both give a family energy for cooking or light. Give one good effect and one harmful effect of each, for the area where you live.
keyIdeas: Charcoal is cheap and works at night, but trees are cut and the smoke harms lungs
Solar is clean and free once bought, but it costs a lot at the start and gives nothing at night
Neither one is only good or only bad
prompts.modelAnswer: Charcoal is cheap, easy to buy in small amounts and burns whenever you need it - but making it means cutting trees, and the smoke in a closed kitchen harms the lungs of whoever cooks. A solar panel makes no smoke and costs nothing to run once you have it, and it can charge a lamp so a child can read at night - but it costs a lot to buy and it makes nothing on a dark evening. Science does not say one is simply good; it tells you what each one costs and who pays it.

prompts.prompt: You are testing which of four materials is the most waterproof. Name the one thing you change and three things you must keep exactly the same, and say what would go wrong if you did not.
keyIdeas: Change only the material
Keep the same: number of drops, height of the drop, same time before checking
If two things change, you cannot tell which one caused the result
prompts.modelAnswer: I change only the material. I keep the number of drops the same, the height I drop them from the same, and the time I wait before checking the same. If I dripped more water on the cloth than on the plastic, the cloth would look worse whether or not it is less waterproof, and I could never tell which of the two things caused it. The things you hold still are what make the one thing you change mean something.

prompts.prompt: You time an ice cube melting and get 11 minutes. Your friend does the same test and gets 14 minutes. Neither of you did anything wrong. What should you do next, and why does it help?
keyIdeas: Repeat the measurement several times
One measurement can be out by chance
Repeats show which numbers are typical and which are odd
prompts.modelAnswer: We should each repeat the test two or three more times and look at all the numbers together. A single measurement can be out by chance - a slightly bigger cube, a warmer spot on the table, a slow start on the stopwatch - and from one number you cannot tell a real difference from an accident. With repeats you can see which times are typical and spot one that is oddly far from the rest, which is what makes the data more reliable.

prompts.prompt: You could record the melting ice as 'it got warmer', or as 4 °C, then 9 °C, then 16 °C on a thermometer. Give two things the degrees let you do that 'it got warmer' does not.
keyIdeas: Degrees mean the same to everyone
You can say how much it changed, not just that it did
Someone else can repeat the measurement and compare
prompts.modelAnswer: First, 9 °C means the same thing to anyone who reads it, while 'warmer' depends on whose hand is doing the feeling. Second, I can say how much it changed - 12 degrees in six minutes - and put those numbers in a table or a graph and see the pattern. And because the unit is standard, someone in another town can repeat my measurement and compare it with mine, which they could not do with 'warmer'.

prompts.prompt: Nobody has ever been to the Earth's core, or even seen it. How can scientists describe what it is made of, and what would make them change that description?
keyIdeas: Earthquake waves travel differently through different materials
The description is built from evidence, not from seeing
New evidence can change it
prompts.modelAnswer: Earthquakes send waves right through the Earth, and those waves speed up, slow down and bend depending on what they pass through, so scientists read the waves that arrive on the far side and work backwards to what the inside must be like. The description is built from evidence, not from looking - which is also why it can change: if new measurements did not fit, scientists would have to change the picture, and they have before. Understanding changes over time because the evidence does.

prompts.prompt: This unit is about volcanoes, earthquakes and habitats. Name two ways this science is used in your own area, and say who uses it.
keyIdeas: Builders and planners use it to decide where and how to build
Rangers and guides use habitat science on the savanna and the reef
Warning services use earthquake and tsunami science on the coast
prompts.modelAnswer: People who plan buildings use it to decide where to build and how, because ground that shakes needs a different kind of wall. On the coast, warning services watch for undersea earthquakes so they can warn people before a tsunami arrives. And rangers and guides use habitat science every day on the savanna and the reef, deciding which areas to protect. The science in this unit is somebody's job within a day's drive of you.

prompts.prompt: Somebody wants to clear a stretch of mangrove to build on. Use what you know about habitats to argue your side, and make sure every point you make rests on science rather than on how you feel.
keyIdeas: Mangrove roots hold the soil and slow waves
Young fish shelter in mangrove roots
Losing it affects the fishing and the shoreline, not only the trees
prompts.modelAnswer: I would argue against clearing it, and every point is a fact rather than a feeling. Mangrove roots hold the soil and slow the water, so the shoreline behind them is protected in a storm; take them away and the sea reaches further in. Young fish shelter among those roots until they are big enough for open water, so fewer mangroves means fewer fish for the people who fish there. Those are reasons anyone can check, which is what makes them worth more in an argument than saying the trees are nice.

prompts.prompt: On the table are a torch, a mirror, a sheet of white card, a sheet of black card, a plastic ruler and a glass of water. You want to show that light travels in straight lines. Which items do you choose, and why do you leave the others?
keyIdeas: Torch and three cards with a hole punched in each
The mirror is for reflection, a different investigation
The glass of water bends light, which would spoil this test
prompts.modelAnswer: I choose the torch and the card, and I punch a hole in three pieces of card and line them up: the light only reaches the far side when all three holes are in a straight line. I leave the mirror, because that shows light bouncing rather than travelling straight, and I leave the glass of water, because water bends light and would make the beam come out somewhere I did not expect. Choosing equipment means knowing what each piece would do to your result.

prompts.prompt: Your question was: which materials let light through? Results: clear plastic - the torch beam passes and you can read through it; greaseproof paper - light passes but you cannot make out the words; card - nothing passes. Write the conclusion so that it answers the question.
keyIdeas: Three groups, not two: transparent, translucent, opaque
Answer the question that was asked
Name the evidence for each group
prompts.modelAnswer: Materials do not simply let light through or not - there are three answers. Clear plastic is transparent, because the beam passed and I could read the words through it. Greaseproof paper is translucent, because light got through but the words did not. Card is opaque, because no light passed at all. The conclusion goes back to the question and gives the evidence for each group.

prompts.prompt: You are building a circuit with a cell, wires and a bulb. Name two risks in this work and the rule that deals with each, then say what you would do if a wire got hot.
keyIdeas: Never use mains electricity from a wall socket - only a small cell
Do not join the two ends of the cell with just a wire
If a wire gets hot, disconnect the cell and tell an adult
prompts.modelAnswer: The first risk is mains electricity, and the rule is that I never put anything of mine into a wall socket - I use only a small 1.5 volt cell. The second is a short circuit: joining the two ends of the cell with only a wire makes the wire heat up fast, so every circuit I build has the bulb in the loop. If a wire got hot I would take the cell out of the holder first, not pull the wire, and then tell an adult. Identifying the risk is what tells you which rule you need.

prompts.prompt: You lit one bulb with one cell, then two cells, then three, and recorded the brightness as dim, bright, very bright. Then you added bulbs instead: one bulb bright, two bulbs dimmer, three dimmer still. Describe both patterns and say how they differ.
keyIdeas: More cells means brighter
More bulbs in one loop means dimmer
One pattern rises, the other falls
prompts.modelAnswer: More cells made the bulb brighter each time, so that pattern rises as the number goes up. More bulbs in the same loop made every bulb dimmer, so that pattern falls as the number goes up. They differ in direction: adding cells adds push to the circuit, while adding bulbs shares the same push among more of them. Describing a pattern means saying which way it goes, and these two go opposite ways.

prompts.prompt: You want to know where the electricity in your town is actually generated, and you cannot go and look. How would you research it, and how would you check the answer is sound?
keyIdeas: Ask at home or at school, look at a bill, read the utility's information
Look for two sources that agree
Prefer the organisation that does the generating
prompts.modelAnswer: I would start with an electricity bill or the power company's own information, ask an adult at home, and look it up in a book or a trusted website about my country's power. Then I would see whether two different sources say the same thing, and give most weight to the company that actually does the generating. Research is a real kind of enquiry, and checking one source against another is what stops it being a rumour.
